title: Quasi-stationary and quasi-ergodic distributions in the Pelikan random map
abstract: In this paper we present a concrete example of a substochastic discrete-time Markov chain on a countable state space producing a spectrum of infinitely many quasi-stationary distributions (QSDs) for generic parameter values, with each QSD supporting a distinct escape rate. Our system is motivated by an open variant of the Pelikan dynamical system, a random map introduced in the 1980s. These QSDs, and their stability to perturbative random noise, are tested in numerical simulations. The existence of unique QEDs is also established for some parameter values.
summary: The paper analyzes the long-term behavior of a random process modeled after an open dynamical system. It rigorously determines the existence and structure of quasi-stationary distributions (QSDs) and quasi-ergodic distributions (QEDs). The key finding is that stable, normalizable QEDs only exist when the underlying Markov chain is in a specific R-recurrent regime.
main_problem: The paper investigates quasi-stationary and quasi-ergodic distributions for a substochastic Markov chain derived from an open variant of the Pelikan random map.
main_result: The system exhibits infinitely many QSDs for generic parameters, and a normalizable QED only exists in the R-recurrent regime; otherwise, theoretical calculations diverge or fail to match simulations.
method: Analysis involves solving eigenvalue problems related to the transfer operator ($M\mu^* = \lambda\mu^*$) and using generating functions (Vere-Jones formalism) to determine recurrence/transience properties.
model_or_system: The model is a biased random walk on the half-line, described by a substochastic discrete-time Markov chain with specific transition probabilities incorporating sub-stochastic resetting at state 0.
key_observables: Quasi-stationary distributions (QSDs), Quasi-ergodic distributions (QEDs), and the associated escape rate ($\gamma_{esc} = -\ln \lambda$).
important_parameters: The bias parameter $p$, the resetting strength $\epsilon$, and the system's dynamical regime (R-recurrent vs. R-transient).
main_assumptions: It is assumed that the principal escape rate eigenvalue ($\lambda_u$) yields the only normalizable QED, and the analysis relies on formalisms for countable absorbing Markov chains.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the open Pelikan map and its associated Markov chain. Figure 2 maps out R-recurrence/R-transience regimes based on parameters $(p, \epsilon)$. Figure 9 compares theoretical QED calculations against numerical simulations, confirming agreement only in the R-recurrent region.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the general framework for QSDs in open chains to analyzing recurrence properties using generating functions. It then derives explicit functional forms for the QED in different regimes, culminating in a comparison between theory and numerical simulation to delineate the boundaries of stable dynamics.
why_interesting: This work provides rigorous mathematical tools (R-recurrence/transience analysis) to study non-equilibrium steady states (QSDs/QEDs) in open systems, which is highly relevant for modeling dissipation or particle loss in complex physical models beyond standard equilibrium statistical mechanics.

Figure 3. ‘Valid’ and ‘invalid’ values of α, for a range of p, ε. Values of α producing µk ≥0 for all k are shown in green. Invalid α, for which µk < 0 for some k, are shown in red. Plot titles are coloured to indicate the dynamical regions discussed in Sec. 2.2, with R-recurrent parameters shown in blue and R-transient parameters in red. The critical value αc is shown in black, and, where it differs from this, the asymptotic αu derived from the principal escape rate is shown in gold. Below each subplot: a bar indicating the number of iterations required to determine validity/invalidity, according to the colour scale shown on the right of the figure.

Fig. 3 confirms that, when α > αc, the produced distributions are always invalid; this is because of the oscillatory problem discussed above. For α < αc, we may or may not have a valid distribution; we rather observe numerically that they are valid for α ≤αu and invalid otherwise. A corollary of this is that λu is the minimal possible eigenvalue (meaning, the fastest possible escape rate), and all λ > λu are supported by some α.
